sub: From the mystery of consciousness to the call of conscience: eight units that reveal the imprint God has left in the human heart.

units.title: The Mystery of Consciousness
units.sub: The brain is an organ you can see; the felt world of “I” is an inner world no one else can see.

share.v: I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well.

blocks.h: Right now you are reading this line. On the screen there are only tiny points of light, yet you “get” the meaning, and you know that you are reading.

The smell of coffee, the colors of a sunset, the ache of missing someone: all of these are experienced from the inside. Others can measure your heartbeat, but no one can feel it for you. This felt inner world is what we call consciousness.
The spirit of man is Yahweh’s lamp, searching all his innermost parts.
The easy problems and the hard problem
The human brain has roughly 86 billion neurons, linked in an extraordinarily complex network. Scientists can already measure which brain regions are active when we see red or hear a sound.

In 1995 the Australian philosopher David Chalmers pointed out that explaining how the brain recognizes and integrates information and controls behavior is the set of “easy problems” (which are not easy at all). The truly “hard problem” is this: why are these physical processes accompanied by subjective experience?

A thermometer can measure exactly 38 °C, yet it does not “feel hot.” A camera can capture a rose, yet it does not “find it beautiful.” Here lies the mystery of consciousness: between processing information and actually feeling something stands a door we still cannot see through.

As early as 1974 the American philosopher Thomas Nagel asked, “What is it like to be a bat?” We could understand everything about a bat’s echolocation and still not know what it experiences from the inside. Subjective experience seems impossible to exhaust with third-person descriptions alone.

Scientists have proposed many theories of consciousness. In 2025 the journal Nature published a large “adversarial collaboration”: supporters of the two leading theories (Global Neuronal Workspace Theory and Integrated Information Theory) preregistered their predictions, which were then tested with fMRI, MEG and intracranial electrodes in 256 participants. Key predictions of both theories failed to find support. This is not failure but honest progress: consciousness remains a frontier of science.
Let’s look at each claim separately and mark how certain it is.
The human brain has roughly 86 billion neurons.
States of consciousness (waking, sleep, anesthesia) are closely tied to brain activity; brain damage changes conscious experience.
There is currently no agreed theory of how the brain produces subjective experience; the leading theories were not fully supported in the 2025 adversarial test.

Subjective experience is very hard to reduce entirely to the workings of matter. That makes the view that “the mind is real” worth taking seriously, and a personal Creator who is himself spirit naturally explains why conscious minds appear in the universe. Even Nagel, an atheist, argued in 2012 that the materialist account is “almost certainly false.”
Perspectives Room
What exactly is consciousness? Here are two major views side by side.

items.h: Consciousness is entirely brain activity. Daniel Dennett and others argue that so-called irreducible “qualia” are a misunderstanding, and that future neuroscience will eventually explain consciousness.

Subjective experience is a real, irreplaceable dimension that physical description cannot fully capture. Theists hold that the mind comes from God, who is himself spirit; some non-theists propose other options, such as panpsychism.

blocks.h: He placed a “spirit” within us
The Bible says that human beings are not just dust; they also have the breath of life that comes from God.
Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
That you can feel, reflect and know that “I” exist is itself a gift. Inside every person is a world others cannot see, known only to their own spirit and to God.
For who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man, which is in him? Even so, no one knows the things of God, except God’s Spirit.
Be still for one minute and notice that you are “aware”: your breathing, the sounds around you, the thoughts in your heart. The you who is aware was made by God’s own hand.
Reflect: Do I treat myself as nothing more than a machine that works, forgetting that I have a soul that needs God?

Prayer: Lord who made me, thank you for giving me a mind that can feel, think and know you. Let your lamp shine into every corner of my inner life, and turn my heart wholly toward you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Holy Spirit is my guide: the spirit of man is the Lord’s lamp. Each day, be still for a moment and let the Holy Spirit shine into my heart.
Humility overcomes pride: if I cannot even fully explain my own consciousness, I admit that I am limited and let God be God.
People matter more than tasks: everyone around me has an unseen inner world worth respecting; they are not tools for getting work done.

blocks.h: This week: find a family member or friend and, without rushing to give advice, listen closely for ten minutes as they share what they are feeling.
Quiz

quiz.q: What does Chalmers mean by “the hard problem of consciousness”?
o: How many neurons the brain has
Why physical processes are accompanied by subjective experience
quiz.e: The hard problem is not how the brain processes information, but why there is any “feeling” at all.

quiz.q: What was the result of the 2025 adversarial test of two leading theories of consciousness?
o: Key predictions of both theories were partly unsupported
Integrated Information Theory was fully confirmed
It proved that consciousness does not exist
quiz.e: Both theories ran into challenges; consciousness remains a scientific frontier.

quiz.q: According to Genesis 2:7, how did man become “a living soul”?
o: He gradually awakened on his own
He ate fruit from the tree of life
God breathed into his nostrils the breath of life
quiz.e: Human life and the human spirit both come from God.

units.title: Can We Trust Reason?
units.sub: We use reason to think about everything, but why should reason itself be trusted?

share.v: The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge, but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.

blocks.h: Someone says, “I don’t trust any reasoning.” But in saying so, he is reasoning. Even to doubt reason, you must first trust reason.

Even more astonishing, the universe can be understood by human minds. In 1936 Einstein wrote that the eternal mystery of the world is its comprehensibility. (The popular version, “The most incomprehensible thing about the universe is that it is comprehensible,” is a paraphrase.)
The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge, but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.
Two remarkable “just so” facts

First, the human mind can grasp logic and mathematics. Second, the universe actually runs according to mathematics. In 1960 the Nobel Prize–winning physicist Eugene Wigner called this “the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences,” and described it as “a wonderful gift which we neither understand nor deserve.”

Imagine sitting in a room and drawing a map with nothing but pencil and paper. You step outside and find that the mountains and rivers match your map at every point. That is often how it goes with mathematics: structures worked out on paper are later found to describe nature exactly.

For example, in 1928 Paul Dirac wrote down an equation describing the electron. Its solutions implied the existence of a positively charged “anti-electron.” In 1932 Carl Anderson actually found the positron in cosmic rays.

In Miracles, C. S. Lewis put forward the “argument from reason”: if our thoughts are entirely the product of non-rational causes, we have little reason to believe they are true. In 1948 the philosopher Elizabeth Anscombe pointed out flaws in his argument; Lewis humbly accepted the criticism and rewrote Chapter 3 for the revised 1960 edition. That itself is a fine example of intellectual honesty.

The contemporary philosopher Alvin Plantinga proposed the “evolutionary argument against naturalism”: natural selection favors behavior that helps survival, not necessarily beliefs that are true. If naturalism (no God) and evolution are both true, the probability that our cognitive faculties are reliable is low or impossible to assess, so the naturalist loses any guarantee even for his own reasoning. His conclusion: the real conflict is not between science and faith but between science and naturalism.
Mathematics has astonishing predictive power in physics; for example, the Dirac equation predicted the positron, which was discovered later.
Natural selection preserves cognitive abilities that aid survival, but scholars still debate how “aiding survival” relates to “seeing the truth.”

The reliability of reason and the intelligibility of the universe both point to a rational Creator, who made human beings in his image and made the universe with a rational order. This is a philosophical inference.
Perspectives Room

items.h: Philosophers such as Fitelson & Sober argue that Plantinga’s probability reasoning is flawed; others argue that true beliefs usually aid survival, so evolution is enough to explain why reason is broadly reliable.
Even if true beliefs often aid survival, this still assumes a world with a stable, intelligible order. Theism holds that mind and universe come from the same wise God, so their fit is no coincidence.

blocks.h: A mind made in God’s image
God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

Many early scientists believed the universe has order because the God who made it is faithful, and that humans can understand the universe because they are made in God’s image. Reason is not the enemy of faith; it is God’s gift for knowing the truth.
You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.
Think of what you have used reason for today: balancing accounts, making plans, understanding a paragraph. Every act of thinking is using a gift from God.
Reflect: Do I use reason to seek the truth, or to find excuses for what I already want to do?
Prayer: God of wisdom, thank you for giving me a mind that can think. Renew my mind, so that my reason bows to your truth and is lit by your Word. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: reason is a good tool, and God’s Word is the measuring line. Let my thinking happen in the light of Scripture.
Changing our mindset changes our lives: from “information” to “revelation,” ask the Holy Spirit to turn head knowledge into heart conviction.
Humility overcomes pride: the fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge; the more I learn about the universe, the more I admit my limits.

blocks.h: This week: write down one question about faith you have had recently, study a related Bible passage, and talk it through with a spiritual companion.
Quiz

quiz.q: What did Wigner mean by “unreasonable effectiveness”?
o: That mathematics describes nature so accurately
quiz.e: Mathematics worked out on paper often turns out to describe the universe exactly.

quiz.q: How did C. S. Lewis respond to Anscombe’s criticism?
o: He humbly accepted it and rewrote a chapter of the book
quiz.e: He rewrote Chapter 3 in the revised 1960 edition, an example of intellectual honesty.

quiz.q: Where does Plantinga say the real conflict lies?
quiz.e: He argues that science fits with theistic belief; the conflict is between science and naturalism.

units.title: The Moral Law Written on the Heart
units.sub: A child’s untaught cry of “That’s not fair!” reveals a measuring rule within the heart.

share.v: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?

blocks.h: Two children are splitting a cake, and the younger one immediately shouts, “That’s not fair!” No one ever taught him a definition of fairness, yet he knows a line has been crossed.
C. S. Lewis noticed that when people quarrel, they rarely say, “I’m stronger than you.” They say, “You shouldn’t do that.” Both sides quietly appeal to the same standard.

For when Gentiles who don’t have the law do by nature the things of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves, in that they show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience testifying with them, and their thoughts among themselves accusing or else excusing them.
A morality shared across cultures

In 2019 a research team at the University of Oxford analyzed ethnographic records from 60 societies and found seven cooperative behaviors regarded as good in the societies studied: helping family, helping your group, returning favors, courage, deference to superiors, dividing resources fairly, and respecting others’ property. They found no society that regarded these behaviors as bad; cultures differed only in how they ranked them.

The world’s musical styles vary endlessly, yet they are all built on a few shared intervals and rhythms. Morality is like that: each culture plays a different tune, but beneath them lies the same “scale.”

In Book One of Mere Christianity, C. S. Lewis argues that the moral law is not merely instinct, because when two instincts clash (the urge to help someone and the urge to protect yourself), something inside tells us which one to follow. Nor is it merely social convention, because we say that one society’s morality is better than another’s, which means there is a standard higher than every society.

A 2007 experiment reported that infants aged 6 to 10 months preferred a “helper” puppet over a “hinderer” puppet. But a large 2025 replication across 37 laboratories with 567 infants did not reproduce this preference. We should not present a single study as settled fact.
In ethnographies of 60 societies, seven cooperative behaviors were widely regarded as good; the researchers note that more detailed tests with new data are still needed.
Whether infants are born making moral evaluations is currently unclear: the original study reported a preference, but a large replication failed to reproduce it.
If there is a universal, objective moral law binding on everyone, the best explanation is a good Lawgiver. This is C. S. Lewis’s famous moral argument.
Perspectives Room
Where do moral intuitions come from? Can they tell us what is truly right and wrong? Here are two major views side by side.

items.h: Moral intuitions may be products of evolution that promote cooperation. The philosopher Sharon Street goes further: if so, we have little reason to believe our moral intuitions reflect objective moral truth.

Evolution can explain “how” we came to have a moral sense, but not that “harming the innocent really is wrong.” If morality is only a survival strategy, that statement loses its real weight, a conclusion most people cannot accept. Theism provides a foundation for objective morality.

blocks.h: A righteous God writes his law on human hearts
Paul says that even people without the law have a conscience bearing witness within them. This standard was not invented by humans; it was engraved by the God who made us.
He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?

Yet knowing what is good is not the same as doing it. Every one of us has gone against the standard in our own hearts. This standard points not only to a Lawgiver; it also shows us that we need salvation.
Recall a moment when seeing injustice made your heart burn. That righteous anger reflects God’s righteous character.
Reflect: I measure others strictly by the standard in my heart. Am I just as honest when I measure myself?

Prayer: Righteous and good God, thank you for writing your law on my heart. Forgive me where I have knowingly done wrong, and give me strength to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: conscience needs to be calibrated by God’s Word; let Scripture be my final standard of right and wrong.
920 (living out the ninefold fruit of the Spirit): morality is not just rules but living out the Spirit’s fruit of goodness, faithfulness and gentleness in relationships.
Humility overcomes pride: measure myself with this standard first, then others.

blocks.h: This week: each evening, take three minutes to review the day: was there something I knew I should do but didn’t? Confess it to God and make it right the next day.
Quiz

quiz.q: What did the Oxford team find in 60 societies?
o: Every society’s morality is completely different
Seven cooperative behaviors are widely regarded as good
quiz.e: Cultures rank them differently, but all seven cooperative behaviors are regarded as good.

quiz.q: What is the current status of research on infants preferring “helpers”?
o: No one has ever studied it
A large replication failed to reproduce it; the evidence is mixed
quiz.e: A 2025 study across 37 labs did not reproduce the original result.

quiz.q: According to Romans 2:15, where is the work of the law written?
quiz.e: “They show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience testifying with them.”

units.title: Free Will and Responsibility
units.sub: A programmed “I love you” is not love; love requires a real choice.

share.v: Choose today whom you will serve … but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.

blocks.h: An engineer could design a robot that says “I love you” right on time every day. But no one would be moved by it, because it cannot choose not to say it.
Love is precious precisely because it could be withheld, yet is freely given. When God made human beings, he gave them the ability to choose.
I call heaven and earth to witness against you today that I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse. Therefore choose life, that you may live, you and your descendants.
Did the brain move first?

In 1983 the neuroscientist Benjamin Libet asked participants to flex their wrist whenever they felt like it and to note the position of a clock at the moment they “decided to move.” He found that brain activity called the “readiness potential” began several hundred milliseconds before the moment participants were aware of deciding. Many people concluded from this that free will is only an illusion.

A ship at sea is constantly pushed by wind and waves; that is real. Yet the helmsman is still at the wheel, setting the course. The brain’s mechanisms are like the wind and waves: real, but not necessarily replacing the one at the helm.

Things are not that simple. Libet himself believed that consciousness can still “veto” an impulse before the action. In 2012 Aaron Schurger and colleagues proposed a model in which the readiness potential may simply be the build-up of the brain’s spontaneous fluctuations, triggering the action only when it crosses a threshold, and does not mean that “the decision was already made.”

Moreover, these experiments study movements like “flick your hand whenever you like,” actions with no reason and no consequences. The truly important choices in life, such as whether to forgive or whether to keep a promise, often involve long reflection and struggle. The two are very different.
Before spontaneous movements, a readiness potential can be measured in the brain, and it appears before participants are aware of deciding.
Neuroscientists still debate whether the readiness potential represents a “decision” or a “build-up of random fluctuations.”

If humans had no choice at all, moral responsibility, genuine love and rational thought would all lose their meaning. Real human choice fits the teaching that humans are made in God’s image. C. S. Lewis argued that by giving humans free will God made evil possible, but also made possible the only kind of love worth having.
Perspectives Room

items.h: Every choice is determined by prior causes; freedom is only a feeling. Critics point out that this makes it hard to ground moral responsibility.
As long as an action comes from your own will and is not forced by outside pressure, it is free; freedom and causation can coexist. Many Reformed theologians hold a similar view.

In the very same situation, a person truly could have chosen otherwise. Many theologians in the Arminian tradition hold this view. Evangelicals differ on this question, but all affirm that people are accountable to God for their choices.

blocks.h: Love needs freedom; freedom is for love
God could have made a world where no one could go wrong, and no one could love. Instead he chose to make a world where people can say “no,” because he wanted children, not machines.
For you, brothers, were called for freedom. Only don’t use your freedom for gain to the flesh, but through love be servants to one another.
Our love is a response to God’s loving us first.
We love him, because he first loved us.
Think about it: what choice today could you use to express love for God and for others?
Reflect: Do I often blame my choices on circumstances, genes or other people, unwilling to take responsibility?

Prayer: Lord Jesus, thank you for giving me the freedom to choose. Today I choose once again to let you reign. May my freedom not become an excuse for indulgence, but a way to serve others in love. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: Let Jesus reign: the best use of freedom is to freely hand the throne to Jesus.
Deny yourself: true freedom is not doing whatever you want, but being able to choose love and service.
Review and correction: take responsibility for your choices; when wrong, admit it, correct course and start again.

blocks.h: This week: pick one thing you have always blamed on other people or your circumstances, write down “one choice I can make,” and act on it this week.
Quiz

quiz.q: What did Libet’s experiment find?
o: The readiness potential appears several hundred milliseconds before the conscious decision
Humans have no freedom at all
The brain is not involved in making decisions
quiz.e: But what it means is still debated.

quiz.q: How did Schurger and colleagues explain the readiness potential?
o: It is a signal from the soul
It may simply be a build-up of the brain’s spontaneous fluctuations
quiz.e: This calls into question the claim that “the decision was already made.”

quiz.q: Why do we say love requires freedom?
o: Because freedom matters more than love
“Love” that is forced or programmed is not true love
Because God doesn’t care about human choices
quiz.e: Choosing to love when you could choose not to is what real love is.

units.title: Longing for Eternity
units.sub: Nothing in this world can fill the human heart, because the heart was made for eternity.

share.v: He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end.

blocks.h: You finally get something you have long hoped for, yet the happiness quickly fades. When you see a magnificent starry sky or hear moving music, an inexpressible longing wells up, as if you were homesick for a home you have never visited.
More than sixteen hundred years ago, Augustine opened his Confessions by telling God, in essence: you made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you (paraphrased).
He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end.
Three longings of the human heart

items: Meaning: people want not only to live, but to know why they live.
Beauty: beautiful scenery, music and art move us, yet always leave a longing that says “this isn’t enough.”
Justice: when we see injustice, we long for the day when everything is set right.

blocks.h: The psychiatrist Viktor Frankl was imprisoned in Nazi concentration camps. In Man’s Search for Meaning he recorded that in the worst conditions, those who could find a meaning to live for were often better able to endure.

Babies get hungry because food exists; people get thirsty because water exists. If the human heart has a longing that nothing in this world can satisfy, perhaps that shows we were made for another world.

This is C. S. Lewis’s “argument from desire.” In Mere Christianity he wrote, in essence, that if I find in myself a desire that no experience in this world can satisfy, the most probable explanation is that I was made for another world.

Critics say that wanting something does not mean it exists; people want to fly, for example. Lewis distinguished “natural desires” (such as hunger and sleep, which have corresponding satisfactions) from “fanciful desires” (such as wanting to fly or wanting fairyland). He argued that the longing for eternity belongs to the first kind: it is universal, and nothing in all creation satisfies it. This is still a philosophical inference, not a proof.
Frankl survived the concentration camps; the German original of Man’s Search for Meaning was published in 1946.
The search for meaning affects a person’s ability to face suffering. This is the core claim of Frankl’s “logotherapy,” and it inspired later research in the psychology of meaning.
The human heart has a longing that created things cannot satisfy; the best explanation is that we were made for the eternal God. This is C. S. Lewis’s argument from desire.
Perspectives Room

items.h: The longing for eternity may be a by-product of evolution or psychology, a wish that humans project outward, which does not mean eternity really exists.
A longing that is universal, deep and never satisfied in this world looks more like something pointing to its true object. Ecclesiastes says it is God who set eternity in the human heart.

blocks.h: Pleasures forevermore in his presence
In Ecclesiastes, the Hebrew word here means “forever.” God placed a longing for eternity in the human heart so that we would not be content with temporary things, but would come and seek him.
You will show me the path of life. In your presence is fullness of joy. In your right hand there are pleasures forever more.
while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.
Who do I have in heaven? There is no one on earth who I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart fails, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.
Recall a beautiful moment that made you think, “I want more.” Bring that longing before God and acknowledge that only he can satisfy it.
Reflect: What have I recently tried to use to fill the emptiness in my heart?

Prayer: Eternal God, you have set eternity in my heart. Forgive me for seeking satisfaction from temporary things. Let me find fullness of joy in your presence, and fix my eyes on the eternal things that cannot be seen. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: From the temporary to the eternal: measure today’s time, money and energy with eternity in view.
Let Jesus receive all the glory: every good thing is a signpost pointing to him; don’t mistake the signpost for the destination.
Give thanks in everything: thank God in every beautiful moment, and let enjoyment become worship.

blocks.h: This week: list three things you have recently poured the most energy into, and ask yourself: a hundred years from now, which of them will still matter? Adjust one, and give that time to eternal things.
Quiz

quiz.q: According to Ecclesiastes 3:11, what has God set in human hearts?
quiz.e: “He has also set eternity in their hearts.” The Hebrew word means “forever.”

quiz.q: What is the main inference of C. S. Lewis’s argument from desire?
o: People want to fly, so people can fly
A longing this world cannot satisfy suggests we were made for another world
quiz.e: This is a philosophical inference, not a strict proof.

quiz.q: What did Frankl observe in the concentration camps?
o: Those who found a meaning to live for were often better able to endure
Physical strength was the only factor
Meaning had nothing to do with survival
quiz.e: He later developed “logotherapy.”

units.title: Language: A Bridge Between Minds
units.sub: With a limited set of words we can say an unlimited range of things; this bridge links one heart to another.

share.v: The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only born Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.

blocks.h: The sentence you are reading right now has very likely never been written in exactly this way before, yet you understand it at once.

A few dozen sounds and a few thousand words can produce an unlimited number of new sentences: about the past, the future, things never seen, love and truth. Through language, the meaning in one heart travels into another.

In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made.
What makes human language unique

items: Unlimited combinations: a limited set of words plus grammatical rules can build an unlimited number of sentences, nested layer upon layer.
Talking about what isn’t here: the past, the future, abstract justice and hope can all be put into words.
Everyone can learn it: the world has more than seven thousand languages, and every normally developing child learns the language around them within a few years.

blocks.h: LEGO bricks come in only a few dozen shapes, yet they can build an endless variety of creations. Language is the same: limited parts, unlimited creativity.

In the 1970s the psychologist Herbert Terrace taught a chimpanzee named “Nim” sign language. Nim learned many signs, but when the team carefully analyzed the videotapes, they found that most of his signs imitated his trainers, and he did not produce grammatically structured sentences.

In 2002 Marc Hauser, Noam Chomsky and Tecumseh Fitch proposed in Science that “recursion,” the ability to nest structures layer upon layer, may be the uniquely human core of language. Animals also communicate in rich ways, such as the honeybee’s dance and monkeys’ alarm calls, but there is currently no evidence that they have this kind of open-ended, infinitely combinable grammar. How language originated remains one of the hardest questions in science.
There are more than seven thousand living languages in the world.
Animals have rich communication systems, but trained apes have not shown the kind of grammatical, infinitely combinable language that humans have.
Scholars still debate how the human capacity for language originated and whether recursion is truly its uniquely human core.

The Bible says, “In the beginning was the Word”: God is a God who speaks and communicates. That humans can express meaning and build relationships through language is best explained by our being made in the image of this speaking God. This is a philosophical and theological inference.
In the beginning was the Word
The “Word” in John’s Gospel is the Greek logos, meaning both word and reason. God created all things through his word, and through his word he reveals himself to us.
God gave Adam the task of naming, and for the first time a human being used language to take part in God’s creation.

Out of the ground Yahweh God formed every animal of the field, and every bird of the sky, and brought them to the man to see what he would call them. Whatever the man called every living creature became its name.
Most wonderful of all, the Word himself became human and lived among us, so that we could know God.
The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only born Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.
Read John 1:14 slowly. The Word who created language came in person among us to speak to us.
Reflect: Lately, have my words been building people up or tearing them down?
Prayer: Word made flesh, thank you for coming in person to speak to me. Cleanse my lips, so that my words carry grace and truth and become a blessing to others. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: God speaks through his Word; read Scripture every day and let his words become my words.
920 (living out the ninefold fruit of the Spirit): let my words bear the Spirit’s fruit of love, kindness and gentleness.
Multiplication: language is a bridge between hearts; use it to pass the gospel on to the next person.

blocks.h: This week: every day this week, use one specific sentence to affirm or bless someone, such as a family member, a coworker, or a brother or sister in your fellowship.
Quiz

quiz.q: What is one of the most distinctive features of human language?
o: It can only talk about what is present
A limited set of words can form unlimited sentences
quiz.e: Nested, unlimited combination is the hallmark of human language.

quiz.q: What did the study of Nim the chimpanzee find?
o: His signs were mostly imitation, and he did not produce grammatical sentences
quiz.e: Terrace’s team reached this conclusion after carefully analyzing the videotapes.

quiz.q: According to John 1:14, what did the Word become?
quiz.e: “The Word became flesh, and lived among us.”

units.title: Made for Love: Persons and Relationships
units.sub: We need relationships the way we need air, because the God who made us is himself a fellowship of love.

share.v: We love him, because he first loved us.

blocks.h: Since 1938, Harvard University has followed a group of people across their whole lives, one of the longest studies of adult development ever conducted. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, sums it up: one of the keys to health and happiness is warm, good relationships.
Not wealth, not fame, but having people who love you, and loving them in return.
Yahweh God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.”
Relationships are a human necessity

In 1958 the psychologist Harry Harlow gave baby monkeys a choice between two “surrogate mothers”: one made of wire and holding a milk bottle, the other covered in soft cloth with no milk. The baby monkeys spent most of their time clinging to the cloth mother, going to the wire mother only when hungry to drink.
A glowing coal left in the fire keeps burning hot; pull it out on its own and it soon goes cold. People are like that: cut off from loving relationships, the heart slowly grows cold.

The British psychiatrist John Bowlby proposed “attachment theory”: children need a stable emotional bond with their caregivers. Mary Ainsworth designed the “Strange Situation” procedure, observing how young children respond when separated from and reunited with a caregiver, and identified secure and insecure patterns of attachment.

A 2010 meta-analysis combining 148 studies and 308,849 participants found that people with stronger social relationships had about a 50% greater likelihood of survival over the follow-up period. This is correlational research and cannot directly prove cause and effect, but it shows that relationships and health are closely linked.
In Harlow’s experiments, baby monkeys preferred to cling to the cloth surrogate mother that offered contact comfort, not just to the one that provided food.
People with stronger social relationships have a higher likelihood of survival (an odds ratio of about 1.5 in the meta-analysis); this is a correlation, and the mechanisms are still being studied.
Early attachment patterns are linked to later relationships, but scholars still debate how large the effect is and whether it can change; attachment is not fixed for life.

Humans have a deep need for love and relationship, which fits the Bible’s revelation: we are made in the image of the triune God, and before creation there was already love among the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. This is a theological and philosophical inference.
The triune God: an eternal fellowship of love
God said, “Let’s make man in our image, after our likeness …”

God says “let us” make man in “our” image. Christians believe that the one God exists in three persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Before the world was made, love was already flowing within God.
… for you loved me before the foundation of the world.
So “God is love” is not a slogan. A solitary god would need creatures in order to love; but the triune God has always been love from eternity. We long for love because we are made in his image.
God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him.
Think of someone who once loved you unconditionally, and thank God for them. That love was a reflection of God’s love.
Reflect: Lately, have I treated tasks as more important than people, and things as more important than relationships?
Prayer: Triune God, you are love, and you made me in your image. Fill me with your love, so that I first draw near to you and can then sincerely love the people around me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The order of relationships: God → self → others → tasks. Draw near to God first, and then you can love others in a healthy way.
235 (three kinds of spiritual relationships): we need spiritual companions, spiritual parents and children, and comrades in arms; don’t walk the road of faith alone.
People matter more than tasks: in the middle of busyness, stop first and see the person.

blocks.h: This week: arrange to meet or call a friend or family member you haven’t been in touch with for a while, and give them your full attention, with your phone put away.
Quiz

quiz.q: In Harlow’s experiment, which surrogate mother did the baby monkeys cling to most of the time?
o: The wire mother with the milk bottle
quiz.e: Contact comfort attracted the baby monkeys more than food.

quiz.q: What did the 2010 meta-analysis find social relationships to be associated with?
quiz.e: People with stronger relationships had about a 50% higher likelihood of survival, but this is a correlation.

quiz.q: Why do we say the triune God “has always been love”?
o: Before creation there was love among the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit
quiz.e: “For you loved me before the foundation of the world.” (John 17:24)

units.title: Conscience and Grace
units.sub: Conscience tells us we have done wrong but cannot erase the past; only the cross can cleanse the conscience.

share.v: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

blocks.h: When you do something wrong, even if no one else knows, your heart is still uneasy. Late at night, when all is quiet, it comes back again and again.
Why do we feel this way? Why, even when we try to convince ourselves that “it’s fine,” does conscience refuse to be quiet?
because if our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and knows all things.
Guilt and shame

Research by the psychologist June Tangney and colleagues distinguishes two feelings: guilt focuses on “I did a bad thing” and often leads to apology and repair; shame focuses on “I am a bad person” and often makes people want to hide, deny or lash out.

Conscience is like a warning light on a car’s dashboard. Pulling out the bulb won’t fix the engine, and staring at the light while blaming yourself won’t fix the car either. What you need is a mechanic who can fix the engine.

Research also shows that healthy guilt is often linked to empathy and responsible behavior, while chronic shame is associated with more psychological distress. This resembles the Bible’s picture: God wants us to confess our actions, but not to be crushed by condemnation.

Psychology can help people deal with unhealthy shame, but there is one thing it cannot do: declare, “Your sins are forgiven.” Forgiveness can only be given by the one who was wronged. Deep down, our conscience knows that the one we have ultimately wronged is the God who wrote his law on our hearts.
Guilt (focused on behavior) more often leads to repair; shame (focused on the self) more often leads to avoidance and defensiveness.
Even without outside punishment, people feel uneasy when they violate their own moral standards; “moral emotions” such as guilt and shame have long been studied in psychology.

Conscience universally points to a moral Lawgiver and Judge, and also makes us long for someone who can forgive. The Christian faith proclaims that this Forgiver is Jesus, who bore our sins on the cross. This is a theological inference and proclamation.
The cross: where the conscience is cleansed
God is righteous and cannot treat sin as if it never happened; God is loving and does not want us crushed by sin. At the cross, righteousness and love meet.
But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without defect to God, cleanse your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?
“Come now, and let’s reason together,” says Yahweh: “Though your sins are as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow. Though they are red like crimson, they shall be as wool.”
So when our conscience accuses us, we don’t need to hide, and we don’t need to punish ourselves. We can come to the cross, confess, and receive complete forgiveness.
There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, who don’t walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit.
Be still for a moment, and honestly bring before God the thing you least want anyone to know. He already knows, and he still loves you.
Reflect: Do I deal with guilt through denial, busyness or self-punishment, or do I come to the cross?

Prayer: Lord Jesus, thank you for shedding your blood and giving your life for me. I confess my sins; forgive me according to your promise and cleanse my conscience, so that I no longer live under condemnation but serve you in your grace. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: Humility overcomes pride: confession is returning to our proper place, letting humans be human and letting God be God.
Selflessness (the self-emptied life): it is no longer I, but Christ living in me; those who have been forgiven learn to forgive others.
Become an overcomer: in Christ there is no condemnation; rely on the Holy Spirit every day to overcome the grip of sin.

blocks.h: This week: confess to God one thing you have been carrying in your heart; if you have wronged someone, take the initiative this week to apologize and make amends.

Congratulations on completing the Mind Hall! From consciousness, reason, morality and freedom to longing, language, relationships and conscience, you have seen a God who gives us minds, writes his law on our hearts, and came in person to cleanse our consciences.
Quiz

quiz.q: What is the main difference between guilt and shame?
o: Guilt focuses on behavior; shame focuses on the self
quiz.e: Guilt says “I did wrong”; shame says “I am bad.”

quiz.q: According to Hebrews 9:14, what can cleanse our conscience?
quiz.e: “How much more will the blood of Christ … cleanse your conscience from dead works.”

quiz.q: According to 1 John 1:9, if we confess our sins, what will God do?
o: Forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness
Require us to make up for them before forgiving
quiz.e: Because God is faithful and righteous.

questions.q: Why can nothing in this world truly satisfy my heart?
If I am only a brain, can I still freely love?
